statement: In BLIS, a 3-parameter saturating model ITL = a + b*rate/(1+d*rate) fits the ITL-rate relationship far better than the paper's 2-parameter model alpha/(1-rho): R2=0.997 (AL) and R2=0.999 (AD) vs R2=0.939 and R2=0.960 respectively. The corrected model MAE is 4.4x smaller (AL) and 5.0x smaller (AD) than the paper model. This holds across all 3 seeds with <0.0001 variance in R2.
regime: qwen/qwen3-14b, 4 instances (2 prefill + 2 decode), 300 requests, prompt=512 tokens, output=128 tokens, rates 1-150 req/s
mechanism: The step-time formula (sim/latency/trained_physics_model.go:321-328) has fixed per-step costs (beta_3*tWeight, beta_5*L=1284us, beta_7=126us) that are amortized over batch size B. Per-token ITL = fixed/B + linear_in_B_per_token. As rate increases, B grows, so fixed/B shrinks, causing ITL to decelerate toward an asymptote. The paper model treats alpha as constant (B-independent), missing this amortization. The 3-parameter model captures F/B+c algebraically: a=isolated ITL at B=1, b/d=asymptotic ceiling above a, d=inverse batch-growth rate.
applicability_bounds: Validated for moderate utilization (rho<0.4). May break down near saturation where queueing effects become dominant. Applies when requests have fixed token lengths (stdev=0).

statement: In BLIS with PD disaggregation, AD (always-disaggregate) TTFT grows only 4.3ms over the full 1-150 req/s range (28% of AL's 15.4ms growth), following a saturating shape with marginals halving from the first half to the second half of the rate range. AL TTFT growth is driven by prefill-decode contention on shared instances.
regime: qwen/qwen3-14b, 4 instances (2 prefill + 2 decode), 300 requests, prompt=512 tokens, output=128 tokens, rates 1-150 req/s
mechanism: In AD mode, dedicated prefill instances handle only prefill traffic, so TTFT is dominated by constant terms: KV transfer (~3.4ms PCIe Gen4), prefill step time (~14ms for 512 tokens). Minor TTFT growth in AD comes from prefill queueing at high rates. In AL mode, prefill requests compete with growing decode batches on shared instances, so each additional unit of load adds scheduling delay to TTFT from both sources.
applicability_bounds: Validated at rates 1-150 req/s where system remains unsaturated (0 drops). TTFT behavior near saturation (when prefill queues build up in AD mode) is uncharacterized.

statement: In BLIS with PD disaggregation, AD achieves lower E2E latency than AL at all tested rates (1-150 req/s), with the E2E benefit growing from 29ms at rate=1 to 255ms at rate=150. The TTFT penalty (15.7ms at rate=1, shrinking to 4.6ms at rate=150) never exceeds 16ms and stays well within a 20ms operational budget. AD is E2E-superior to AL across the entire moderate-load regime for this workload.
regime: qwen/qwen3-14b, 4 instances (2 prefill + 2 decode), 300 requests, prompt=512 tokens (fixed), output=128 tokens (fixed), rates 1-150 req/s
mechanism: The E2E benefit has two drivers: (1) Growing ITL benefit (0ms at rate=1 rising to 1.69ms per token at rate=150) accumulated over 127 decode tokens, overwhelmingly exceeds (2) the shrinking TTFT penalty (15.7ms->4.6ms). Both effects arise from dedicated disaggregated instances: AD decode instances avoid prefill interference, enabling larger decode batches and better amortization. AD prefill instances handle only prefill, keeping TTFT growth minimal while AL's shared instances develop both TTFT and ITL penalties at high rates.
applicability_bounds: Validated for fixed-length requests (prompt=512, output=128, stdev=0). The E2E plateau at ~255ms above rate=130 suggests the ITL benefit saturates (both modes approach their asymptotic ceilings). The 20ms TTFT budget margin was probed down to rate=1; with shorter output lengths the ITL benefit would be smaller and the TTFT penalty would dominate at low rates.

statement: In BLIS, always-disaggregate (AD) yields consistently lower mean inter-token latency (ITL) than always-local (AL) across all tested arrival rates (10-150 req/s), with the ITL advantage growing monotonically from 0.13ms at rate=10 to 1.69ms at rate=150. At rate=1, ITL advantage is 0ms (both modes process one request at a time, batch size=1). The advantage is zero at rate=1 because disaggregation requires concurrent decode requests to benefit from batch-size amortization.
regime: qwen/qwen3-14b, 4 instances (2 prefill + 2 decode), 300 requests, prompt=512 tokens, output=128 tokens, rates 1-150 req/s
mechanism: AD decode instances are not interrupted by prefill requests, achieving larger decode batches that amortize fixed per-step costs (sim/latency/trained_physics_model.go:321-328). At rate=1, only one request is in flight at any time (arrival rate << service rate), so both AL and AD process single requests with batch size=1, yielding identical ITL. The benefit emerges only when concurrent requests can be batched together.
applicability_bounds: Validated for rates 1-150 req/s. At rate=1, ITL advantage is exactly 0ms (no batching). Advantage grows with rate up to ~130 req/s, then plateaus.

statement: In BLIS, always-disaggregate (AD) incurs consistently higher mean TTFT than always-local (AL) across all tested arrival rates (1-150 req/s), with a TTFT penalty of 4.6-15.7ms. The penalty is largest at low rates (15.7ms at rate=1) and shrinks to ~4.6ms at high rates as AL's TTFT grows from prefill-decode contention. The constant floor is ~3.4ms KV transfer overhead at 25 GB/s plus constant prefill step time differences.
regime: qwen/qwen3-14b, 4 instances (2 prefill + 2 decode), 300 requests, prompt=512 tokens, output=128 tokens, rates 1-150 req/s
mechanism: TTFT_AD = prefill_scheduling + prefill_step + KV_transfer + first_decode_step. TTFT_AL = scheduling_delay + prefill_step. The difference at low rates is dominated by KV transfer (~3.4ms) and the extra decode step. At high rates, AL's TTFT grows due to prefill-decode contention on shared instances, shrinking the AD-AL gap.
applicability_bounds: Validated for rates 1-150 req/s in unsaturated regime. TTFT penalty floor is ~4.6ms at rate=150 in this configuration.

statement: In BLIS, both AL and AD ITL follow a concave, monotonically increasing function of arrival rate consistent with a saturating model ITL = a + b*rate/(1+d*rate). The corrected model fits with R2=0.997 (AL) and R2=0.999 (AD) over rates 1-150 req/s. The paper's alpha/(1-rho) model achieves R2=0.939 (AL) and R2=0.960 (AD) over the same range. The corrected model's 3 parameters map to physics: a=isolated ITL at B=1, d=inverse batch-growth rate, a+b/d=asymptotic ITL ceiling.
regime: qwen/qwen3-14b, 4 instances (2 prefill + 2 decode), 300 requests, prompt=512 tokens, output=128 tokens, rates 1-150 req/s
mechanism: Overhead amortization in the step-time formula (sim/latency/trained_physics_model.go:321-328): fixed per-step costs (beta_5*L + beta_7 = ~1410us, plus tWeight loading of ~several ms) are divided by batch size B. As rate grows, B grows, amortizing these costs and causing ITL to decelerate toward an asymptote.
applicability_bounds: Validated at moderate utilization (rho<0.4, 0 drops at all rates). The asymptotic ceiling (33ms AL, 31ms AD) is not approached in the tested range.
